The biggest thing about my team is all my options are high volume and high minute players. I usually finish 100-300 more minutes played per week than my opponent. That allows the law of averages to work its magic.

I target volume shooters like top-tier guards and prolific scorers. Even lesser-known players can become very valuable because their free throw percentage impact is very high.

I try to keep as few big men on my roster as possible. Every few weeks I might have to stream a center or power forward to fill a spot, but I stream every day anyway, so who cares?

My pre-draft strategy was to carefully rank exactly who I wanted in order. I wrote out about 100 players who fit my build and ranked them from 1-100, then drafted the best available one from that list when it was my turn.

Also, build around your best player. In my case, I got a top guard with my first pick, so by default, I want to target his strong stats: free throw percentage, points, assists, steals, three-pointers.

If I had a different star player, maybe I wouldn't do a field goal percentage punt, for example.

I firmly believe that it's easier to dominate with a guard-heavy roster because there are so many good ones. It's a lot harder to get talented bigs who fit your build. Plus, rebounds are cheap, so it's easy for your competition to upset that category anyway.

Assists are the hardest category to win, so I always draft those players earlier in the draft and make sure my whole roster averages 3+ assists if possible. That's why a player with solid assist numbers is awesome for my build. His 5 assists a game make a real difference.

Target high minutes per game and low injury risk players, though! That's the only reason my strategy works. A top guard is leading the league in minutes played for two years in a row now. That's why I would take him over other star players in a heartbeat.

Oh, and the last thing is playoff schedule. That's another reason I targeted a player with a favorable schedule.
